paras: The attempted lynching of an Indian prisoner at Fort Colville took place in Washington Territory in mid-March 1881, when citizens marched to take from jail an Indian accused of shooting a man known as Dutch Joe. The military took charge of the prisoner and locked him in the Fort Colville guardhouse, and he was not harmed. The episode reached readers through a Walla Walla wire item, a territorial weekly, and a Pennsylvania paper printing letters from a cavalry officer at the fort.

According to a Walla Walla dispatch of March 21, an Indian had shot and killed Dutch Joe "on sight" a few days earlier, though "there was no trouble between them." That dispatch called the Indian "supposed to be demented." The Vancouver Independent gave a different account, saying the two had quarreled with "very sharp language on both sides" before the Indian drew his pistol and shot his companion.

News of the shooting caused "the wildest excitement" in the town, and crowds of citizens talked of it until they were "thoroughly indignant." They then marched in a body to take the prisoner from jail and lynch him. The authorities sent a messenger to the military, which took charge of the prisoner and locked him in the guardhouse.

Lieutenant Foltz of the 1st U.S. Cavalry, stationed at the fort, gave a fuller account of the authorities' request. In his version, the civil authorities applied to the commandant for protection, saying they could not keep their prisoner from citizens "determined to lynch him." The law required a presidential order before troops could aid civil officers, which would have taken a week, but the people did not know this and "feared to act." The military could hold the prisoner without that order once the officers of the law delivered him, and he was taken to the guardhouse.

No report of arrests among the crowd appears in the coverage, and the March reports do not name the prisoner. In September 1881 an Indian called Andrew "Tenaapa" was sentenced to hang for murdering Gottlieb Reimer in Colville valley "last spring." Briefs in November and December reported that Andrew Tempes had been executed at Fort Colville for murdering a white man. None of these reports mentions Dutch Joe or the lynching attempt, and a San Francisco dispatch dated Tempes's crime "over a year ago," so it is unclear whether this was the same case.

The Daily Los Angeles Herald ran the Walla Walla dispatch on March 24 among Pacific Coast items headed "Two Unpublished Crimes," without comment. A week later the Vancouver Independent printed a longer version that described the town's excitement and the crowd's indignation without condemning or endorsing it. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer used the episode on April 13 as background to Foltz's "felicitous sketches of Indian and Chinese character," saying the Indian "came very near being lynched for his crime."
The later Tempes execution circulated as a one-line brief in papers from New Jersey to Louisiana.

The accounts disagree on the shooting itself: the wire report said there had been no trouble and the man was thought "demented," while the Vancouver Independent described a quarrel first. They also differ on how far the crowd went, from "tried to lynch" in the wire report to Foltz's statement that the people "feared to act."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of an Indian prisoner at Fort Colville
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Citizens of Fort Colville gathered to take a jailed Indian accused of killing Dutch Joe and lynch him, but the military took the prisoner into the guardhouse, so this is an attempted lynching of a Native American, not of a Black person (A2, A3, A4).

The 'crowds of citizens' who marched to take the prisoner from jail to lynch him over the killing of Dutch Joe acted without lawful authority and under a pretext of punishment, but the prisoner was placed in the guardhouse and no one was killed (A2, A3, A4).

A Walla Walla wire report (A2), a Washington Territory paper with a fuller version (A3), and an officer stationed at the fort writing to his family (A4) each describe the threatened lynching and the transfer of the prisoner to the military.

accounts.label: Walla Walla wire report
accounts.gist: An Indian shot Dutch Joe 'on sight' though there was no trouble between them and was 'supposed to be demented'; citizens tried to lynch him but the military locked him in the guardhouse.

accounts.label: Vancouver Independent
accounts.gist: The two men quarreled with 'very sharp language' before the Indian drew a pistol; indignant crowds marched to take him from jail, and the military took charge after the authorities sent a messenger.

accounts.label: Lt. Foltz, via the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer
accounts.gist: The civil authorities asked the commandant for help, saying they could not keep the prisoner from the citizens; the troops could not legally intervene without a presidential order, but the people did not know that and feared to act.

framing.detail: The Herald ran the item without comment under 'Two Unpublished Crimes', calling the accused 'supposed to be demented'.
The Vancouver Independent described 'the wildest excitement' and 'thoroughly indignant' citizens without condemning or endorsing the lynching attempt.
The Lancaster editor treated the episode as background to an officer's 'felicitous sketches of Indian and Chinese character', explaining the legal limits on military aid.

record_check.dossier: The target of the lynching attempt was 'an Indian' (Native American), not a Black person; the episode is outside an anti-Black scope
A march on the jail to seize the prisoner (threat/attempt); no pursuit or siege is reported
'Citizens' / 'the people of the country' of Fort Colville, unnamed
Attempted by the wire and Vancouver accounts; the officer's account says the people 'feared to act'
Three independent accounts, the last on 1881-04-13 (Lancaster Daily Intelligencer)

info: Fort Colville, Washington Territory; the prisoner was held in the jail and then in the Fort Colville guardhouse
An unnamed Indian prisoner, the target of the lynching attempt; he was not harmed
Accused of shooting and killing a man known as Dutch Joe
'Citizens' of the town and 'the people of the country'; no names given
The prisoner was locked in the guardhouse and was not lynched; no later report naming him or his fate was tied to the Dutch Joe killing
